lines: A matcher doesn't output clusters. It outputs scored pairs, one at a time, with no sense of the groups they're about to form. Everything in this topic is about what happens once you start joining them.
Before you answer, notice the question isn't really about clustering. It's about what a threshold actually does to a graph that's already built out of pairwise decisions.
answer: Nothing changes until the threshold crosses that one bridging pair's exact score. Then it jumps.
A pair is either a match or it isn't — there's no partial union. So the cluster count can't move smoothly; it has to be a step function, with one step per bridging edge you cross.

lines: Nothing on this screen is new. The entire point of putting it here is that this chapter already proved it correct once, and you get to spend zero effort re-earning that trust.
Notice what's deliberate about this graph: the within-group pairs are almost all scored high enough that no reasonable threshold would ever drop them. Only the two bridges are built to be fragile.
That's not how a real matcher's scores would look by accident. It's built this way on purpose, so the one effect this topic is about isn't buried in noise.

Read this sentence slowly: it says connected components, not clustering, not grouping, not anything softer. The people who built this tool reached for the exact graph-theory term, because that's exactly what it is.

Watch how long record zero's entity id does nothing at all. That's not a bug in the visualization — it's the actual behavior of a record sitting in a well-connected group, waiting for the rest of the graph to catch up to it.
The two moments it does change are the only two pairs in the whole stream that matter to this specific record. Everything else was already decided.
This is the predict's answer, laid out as it actually happened: two flat stretches, two drops, nothing in between. If you expected a smooth curve, notice exactly where that expectation breaks.
Each drop lines up with crossing one bridge's score, not with any particular number of threshold steps. The x-axis you'd want to draw this against is score, not 'how many thresholds have I tried.'

Ask yourself what would even need to happen for union to have a splitting counterpart. It would need to remember, for every merge, exactly which edge caused it — and union-find was built specifically to not carry that weight.
That's not a missing feature. It's the trade that makes the structure fast in the first place.
Same algorithm, same two lines of code, a completely different question. Nothing about union-find cares whether the vertices are customer records or dataset names.
What changes is what a 'component' means to the person reading the output. Here, it means a blast radius, not an identity.

Think about what a single shared parent array actually requires: every machine needs to be able to see and update the same memory. That assumption is the whole topic in one sentence, and it's the assumption a cluster doesn't get to make.
Before the answer lands, notice this is a real trade, not a hypothetical one — the source names an actual checkpoint interval, which only exists because rounds cost something real.
answer: Many more rounds than union-find's one pass.
Ten rounds of every node talking to its neighbors, to converge on the same answer union-find found by walking the edge list exactly once. The cost isn't correctness — it's communication.

lines: Say the number out loud: ten. Not two, not three. That's the real cost of giving up a shared parent array, measured on a graph with only twenty-four records.
Scale this graph up and the gap doesn't close — it's the structural reason distributed connected-components implementations exist as their own research area at all.
Carry forward the shape of the lesson, not just the algorithm: a structure's guarantees come from what it refuses to support. Union-find is fast because it never promised to split.
